dossier.public_summary: The dip changes from about 1200 ppm in a few sectors to near zero in others and individual transit depths scatter to 1700 ppm, with three deep dips dominating the signal. It also shows a deep secondary eclipse at one-third the primary depth. This sector dependence, depth instability and clear secondary favour a false alarm from a background variable system rather than a planet on the bright Sun-like star.

reasons.why: Depth is not steady within the same pipeline: solved depths as high as 1277 ppm in sectors 17, 21, 50 versus essentially zero in sectors 20, 40, 41, 80, 84. A planet must be stable, so the large sector-to-sector change favours a non-planet, blended/variable origin.
Individual transits are wildly inconsistent; three high dips from sector 50, 17 and 21 carry most of the signal. A few bad events dominate a real planet signal, not expected scatter.

reasons.why: A strong secondary at ~0.3248x primary depth is detected at SNR 7.61, as deep as the brightest brightening, with secondary_phase_offset 0.08803. Typical hot Jupiters show <~1% secondaries; this depth matches a stellar eclipse, not a planet.
